newsitem.title: CANADA: Food and cash pour into flood-hit Manitoba.
newsitem.headline: Food and cash pour into flood-hit Manitoba.

text.p: Food, clothes and cash are pouring into flood-stricken Manitoba as people across North America open their hearts to victims of the western Canadian province's worst flood in 145 years.

"I've never seen anything like it in my life. We've been overwhelmed by the support we've got from around the country," Salvation Army spokeswoman Anne Bennett said. "Some people are arriving with nothing but the clothes on their backs and they really need all the support they can get."
More than 12,000 volunteers from Winnipeg and other parts of Canada helped lay sandbags and were feeding and comforting many of the 28,000 Manitoba evacuees, local authorities said.

South of the border in flood-hit North Dakota an anonymous woman offered $2,000 checks to more than 50,000 residents in Grand Forks and East Grand Forks made homeless by flood waters 10 days ago. The donations could total millions of dollars.
Canadian Airlines, Canada's second-biggest, has offered discount tickets to volunteers and has cut rates for care packages destined for Manitoba's flood victims.

"There's a real neat sense of community here. People that are in crisis, it's their neighbours that are coming out to help even though they're the next people in line," local Red Cross spokeswoman Sharilyn Amy said.

The Red Cross call centre has directed 600 phone calls to relocated evacuees from friends and relatives from across Canada and overseas, Amy added. While that organisation placed evacuees, collected individual and corporate cash donations and reunited displaced residents with loved ones, the Salvation Army fed and clothed people.

"In the last two weeks we've been feeding sandbaggers, and now as you can see we're involved here with the reception of clothing and household items for people when they return to their homes," Salvation Army Lt.-Col. David Luginbuhl said as dozens of volunteers unloaded trucks at a recycling warehouse.

Truckloads of clothes and bedding came from across Canada and were being laundered for free by a Winnipeg hotel. The Salvation Army has served more than 40,000 sandwiches and 10,000 canned drinks to 70,000 flood victims and volunteers.

The University of Manitoba opened its children's camp for free, while donated toys crammed a hotel conference room where 120 children sought refuge with their evacuated parents. A Winnipeg animal shelter even offered free space for the pets of flood evacuees.
Word of the devastation in Manitoba has also drawn offers of help from around the world.

"I got a call from the Canadian Embassy in Paris asking how they could help. I got calls from the Netherlands and Germany yesterday. I got a call from a 10-year-old girl in Winnipeg saying she could make sandwiches," Winnipeg Mayor Susan Thompson said. "It's just wonderful."
